(ORAL)
1. Vide this order, I propose to dispose of the present Criminal Appeal filed against the judgment dated 08.07.2016 and order on sentence dated 13.07.2016 passed by Ld. ACMM-II, Patiala House Courts, New Delhi.

Brief facts:
2. That on 16.09.2006, the food officials consisting of Food Inspector (FI) Sh. Rajendra Kumar Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/
1 Bhaskar and Field Assistant (FA) Sh. D.N. Verma under supervision of SDM/LHA Sh. D.S. Gehlot,
reached alongwith their staff at the premises of M/s Gupta Store at E-192, Naraina Vihar, New Delhi-110028, where the appellant was found conducting the business of various food articles which are lying stored/exposed for sale for human consumption.
The FI disclosed his identity and expressed his intention to purchase a sample of 'Pepper Black (Kali Mirch) Whole'.

Sample of the Kali Mirch was purchased and divided into 3 counterparts and were separated packed, fastened,
marked and sealed, as per the provisions of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955.
One counterpart of the sample was sent to Public Analyst (PA) in intact condition and the other two counterparts were deposited with SDM.LHA.
Vide report dated 06.05.2011, the PA found the sample to be adulterated on the ground that it contained mineral oil and exceed the prescribed maximum limit of 5.0%.

Accordingly, after completion of investigation, sanction under Section 20 of the Act was obtained and the complaint was then filed on 03.06.2011 for violation of Section 2 (ia) (a), (b) & (m) of the PFA Act as well as Section 2 (ix)(d) of PFA Act read with Rule 44-AAA Rules, as punishable under Section 7/16 (1)(a) of PFA Act.
3. The appellant was summoned vide order dated 03.06.2011.

An application under Section 13(2) of the Act was filed by the appellant on 18.11.2006 thereby exercising his right to get the second counterpart of the sample analysed from Central Food Laboratory (CFL).
The application was allowed and a counterpart was sent to CFL.

The CFL examined the sample and gave Certificate dated 12.07.2011, opining the sample to be not conforming to the standards of Black Pepper (Kali Mirch) Whole as per PFA Rules due to the presence of mineral oil.

4. On the basis of CFL Report, notice of accusation under Section 251 Cr.P.C. was framed against the accused on 22.12.2011 for commission of offence punishable under Section 7/16(1)(a) of PFA Act,
being violation of Section 2(ia)(a) and (m), to which he pleaded not guilty and claimed trial.
5. The prosecution examined three witnesses namely, PW-1 FI R.K Bhaskar, PW-2 Sh. D.S. Gehlot (the then SDM/LHA) and PW-3 FA Sh. D.N. Verma.
6. The statement of the accused was recorded u/s 313 Cr.P.C. on 16.09.2015 in which he claimed his innocence.

7. Ld. SPP for the Department has argued that the complainant has been able to establish its case against the accused beyond reasonable doubt, on the ground that the accused has not been able to rebut the findings of the CFL report dated 12.07.2011.
It is also submitted that all the witnesses have supported its case and no major contradiction can be seen in their testimony.
It submitted that the present appeal is liable to be dismissed.
8. I have heard the arguments and have perused the record.

A) Delay in analysis and lodging of prosecution:
Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/
2 9.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Ld. Counsel for the appellant has firstly stated that in the present case, the sample was lifted on 16.09.2006.
Thereafter, the report of the public analyst was prepared on 06.05.2011 i.e. about 56 months after the collection of sample.
Counsel has emphasized that the present case pertain to perishable food article Black Pepper (Kali Mirch) and the same does not have very long shelf life.
He has next contented that not only there was delay on this account itself, there was a further delay of almost 1 month in the filing of the complaint.
It was only when, after 1 month, the complaint was filed, the accused got an opportunity to get the second sample tested under Section 13 (2) of PFA Act.

However, due to the delay caused in lodging of prosecution, such valuable right of the accused can be said to have been clearly defeated,
as under no circumstances, Kali Mirch Whole could have been fit for testing/analyzing after such a long period of time.

11. Ld. Counsel has relied upon the decision in State Vs. Vinod Kumar Gupta, 2010 (2) JCC 987,
where lodging of prosecution even after 4 months was rejected on the account of delay as it would defeat the right of the accused for getting the sample tested for the second time.

entities.text: State Vs. Vinod Kumar Gupta, 2010 (2) JCC 987
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
12. Ld. Counsel has, in support of his contention, further relied upon the decision in MCD Vs. Ghisa Ram, Criminal Appeal No. 194/66 in SC of PFA cases 1951-1975 at page 93 and decision in Chanan Lal Vs. State, 1972 PFA Cases 292, as also, Girish Bhai Dahiyabhai Shah Vs. CC Jani, 2009 (2) FAC 194.
13.

entities.text: MCD Vs. Ghisa Ram, Criminal Appeal No. 194/66
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Chanan Lal Vs. State, 1972 PFA Cases 292
entities.label: PRECEDENT

entities.text: Girish Bhai Dahiyabhai Shah Vs. CC Jani, 2009 (2) FAC 194
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
In the present case, the samples were examined by the Public Analyst from 26.04.2011 to 04.05.2011 and by CFL from 02.07.2011 to 12.07.2011.
14.
It may be pertinent to note that the relevant standard is A.05.17 for Black Pepper (Kali Mirch).

Although the PA's report records that the extraneous matter was 0.15%, Light Berries was 5.78%,
Pim Head was 0.10%, moisture was 8.11%, total ash was 4.73%, non-volatile ether extract was 7.21%.

The CFL report which was prepared only a few days after the PA's report found Light Berries as 2.63% i.e. within the limit prescribed and, therefore, at least on this aspect the prosecution initiated on the basis of PA's report must fail.
However, it is worthwhile noticing that the moisture level and other parameters are also different as per the CFL than the report given by the PA.

The difference of more than 3% in the amount of Light Berries in the two reports raises a doubt about the sample being representative and whether the same was properly mixed before the samples were drawn.

15. It appears that the Light Berries may be on the top due to movement during transportation and,
therefore, when the first sample was drawn, the Light Berries were 5.78% and when the second sample was drawn, they were reduced to 2.63%.
Holding both the reports to be correct, there is no other possible explanation for such a large variation in the quantity of Light Berries in the two samples.

16. Further, it may be worthwhile noticing that for almost five years, the samples were not examined and the benefit of the delay must also be given to the accused as Kali Mirch is a perishable product Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/
3 and may undergo the process of decay in ordinary course in the long period of five years.

entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 17. Besides the aspect of delay, it is important to note that the name of method of analysis adopted by both the labs seems to be not inconformity with the other.
Both the labs conducted the testing of the sample after the notification of labs and methods of testing.

However, surprisingly, while PA is referring to DGHS Manual as reference manual for adopting the method of analysis, the CFL is referring to A.O.A.C., I.S5887-III and I.C.M.R. 1990 as reference material.
The prosecution has not led any further evidence as to the contents of DGHS Manual to show that the same test has been prescribed in the literature referred to in both the reports.
It was for the prosecution to show that the method adopted or utilized by the PA and the CFL was in accordance with the notification issued by the Government in this regard.

18. For this it would be relevant to refer to the provisions of Section 23(1A)(ee) and (hh) which read as follows:
"23(1A) In particular and without prejudice to the generality of the foregoing power,
such rules may provide for all or any of the following matters, namely:-
............................
(ee) defining the laboratories where samples of articles of food or adulterants may be analysed by public analysts under this act;
.......................
(hh) defining the methods of analysis
The said provisions were incorporated in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 with effect from 01.04.1976 only through Act 34 of 1976.

20. Through notification dated 25.03.2008 of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare published in the Gazette of India (Extraordinary), in exercise of the powers conferred by Section 23 of the 1954 Act, the Central Government has incorporated Rule 4(9) in the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955, through Prevention of Food Adulteration (Second Amendment) Rules, 2008.

entities.label: ORG

entities.text: Prevention of Food Adulteration (Second Amendment) Rules, 2008
entities.label: STATUTE

sentences.text:
21. The present Rule 4(9) reads as follows:-
"The manuals of method of analysis brought out by Ministry of Health and Family Welfare shall be adopted for analysing the samples food articles.

entities.label: ORG

However, in case the method for analysing any parameter is not available in these manuals, the method of a n a l y s i s

Further, in case of non- availabiltiy of method of analysis in these manuals, the method prescribed in other standard Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/
4 published literature of publication shall be adopted."

entities.text: Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
22. It has to be noted that the said notification has come into force only on 25.03.2008.
23.

These aspects were considered by the Apex Court in the case of Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
vs. Food Inspector & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC (Cri) 8.

entities.text:
Pepsico India Holdings Pvt. Ltd.
vs. Food Inspector & Anr. (2011) 1 SCC (Cri) 8
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In the said case, the point raised for consideration was whether in the absence of any prescribed and validated method of analysis u/s 23 (1a) (hh) of the Act, could a prosecution be launched against the appellants based on the reports submitted by the Public Analyst using the method of the Director General of Health Services (DGHS).

This point was answered in the judgment wherein it was observed that these Sections were not enabling provisions but were mandatory and could be resolved by the Central Government by framing the Rules thereunder, by which specified tests to be held in designated laboratories could be spelled out.
It was further noted that in the absence of such discriminated laboratories and specified tests, it can lead to a pick and choose method to suit the prosecution, which cannot be permitted.
The non-formulation of Rules under these provisions of the Act is, therefore, fatal for the prosecution.

In the Pepsico case (Supra), it was further noted that once there is no information in regard to discriminated reports of the validated methods of analysis, the exercise of sending the second sample to Central Food Laboratory for analysis would be an exercise in futility.

24. This judgment of the Apex Court was followed by the Kerala High Court in the case of R.
Gopalakrishnan Vs. Food Inspector in Criminal Revision Petition No.671/2002 decided on 17.07.2013.

entities.text:
R.
Gopalakrishnan Vs. Food Inspector in Criminal Revision Petition No.671/2002
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was observed that the observations made in the Pepsico case were not limited to the food article i.e. the sample of pepsi that was the subject matter in the said appeal, but it laid down the general preposition of law to be followed in all the cases.
Special Leave Petition against the said judgment was preferred in Supreme Court of India, vide Criminal Appeal No. 2476 of 2014, but the same was dismissed.

25. In a recent judgment of M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015 (2) FAC 56 the Bombay High Court has again followed the Pepsico case (supra)
to observe that in the absence of designated laboratories and validated methods of analysis, the reports of the Public Analyst and the Director, CFL, cannot be relied upon.
26.

entities.text: M/s Nestle India Ltd. Vs. the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India and Ors. 2015 (2) FAC 56
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
Reliance is also placed upon the decision of the Hon'ble Kerala High Court in Mohanan P. &
Others Vs. State of Kerala and Another, Crl. Rev. P.No. 66 of 2011, decided on 25th November, 2021 where the earlier decision in R. Gopalakrishnan (supra) has again been followed.

entities.text:
Mohanan P. &
Others Vs. State of Kerala and Another, Crl. Rev. P.No. 66 of 2011
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
27. Returning to the facts of the present case, it is noteworthy that the PA adopted "DGHS Manual"
method and CFL adopted "A.O.A.C., I.S5887-III and I.C.M.R." method to determine the presence or absence of mineral oil.

28. In Dhian Singh Vs. Municipal Board Saharanpur, AIR 1970 SC 318, the Hon'ble Supreme Court was of the view that the report of the PA need not contain the mode or particular of analysis nor the test applied.

entities.text: Dhian Singh Vs. Municipal Board Saharanpur, AIR 1970 SC 318
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: This decision was rendered before the amendment in the statute, whereby the Parliament decided to incorporate the two sub clauses (ee) and (hh) to Section 23 (1A).
The Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da) on 28 March, 2023 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/117993979/

entities.text: Suresh Kumar Bansal vs . The State (Da)
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: 5 intention of the legislature seemed to be that to obviate any discrepancies in the reports solely on count of the laboratory to which articles were sent or the different test methods adopted by different labs, the said provisions were incorporated.

Therefore, what was not significant prior to 1976,
became relevant and important.
The decision in Dhian Singh (Supra), most respectfully, would cease to be the applicable law on the aspect in view of the specific legislative mandate introduced by way of amendment.

Any subsequent decision, for a case instituted on a sample taken after the amendment of 1976, which fails to note the statutory amendment and follows the aforesaid decision in Dhian Singh (Supra), can be treated as a decision rendered sub silentio.

29. In the absence of any evidence that valid method of examination was used when both reports give different description of method of analysis, it would not be safe to rely on any of the report to conclude that the sample was adulterated.
30. The benefit of the same has to be extended to the appellant.
The conviction and sentence is set aside.
Appellant is acquitted.
Bail bond cancelled.
Surety bond discharged.
Bail bond u/s 437-A Cr.P.C. be furnished.
31. The present criminal appeal is disposed off accordingly.
32. The present appeal is disposed of accordingly.
33. TCR be sent back with the copy of this order.
34. Appeal File be consigned to Record Room.
